description: We are a team based in India focusing on building an innovative solution for NASA Space Apps 2026. For this project, we'll be using NISAR data as well as well as skills related to machine learning and deep learning.
summary:
We built a platform that turns complex satellite radar data into clear, actionable intelligence. Standard optical satellites go blind at night or during heavy storms. To fix this, our system uses NASA and ISRO radar data (SAR) to see straight through thick clouds and dense forest canopies.

Historically, analyzing this kind of telemetry required expensive desktop software and specialized training. We removed that friction by shifting the heavy processing to a cloud pipeline, which delivers interactive 3D maps, machine-learning classifications, and real-time scientific charts directly into a standard web browser.

This matters because it transforms raw physics into ground-level survival tools. Whether it is analyzing flooded villages in Assam during a monsoon, uncovering illegal logging hidden beneath the Amazon canopy, or tracking sinking ground in California to protect infrastructure, our platform gives scientists and governments the exact spatial intelligence they need to act quickly and save lives.
details:
What it does and how it works

We have build a platform that bridges the gap between microwave physics and ground-level disaster response. Standard optical satellites are essentially blind during heavy storms or under dense forest canopies. To solve this, we built a Advanced Radar Geodesy Lab that leverages Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from NASA (L-Band) and ISRO (S-Band) and shared our findings to the public.

The system operates on a split architecture:

  1. The Cloud Engine: A Python script that queries massive 11GB+ HDF5 radar granules via NASA's earthaccess API. To handle the scale, it maps the datasets to dask arrays for lazy loading, computes physical indices like the Radar Vegetation Index (RVI) and dielectric roughness, and runs unsupervised machine learning (K-Means) to physically segment the pixels (e.g., water, canopy, flooded trees).
  2. The Web Interface: The Python script then exports lightweight GeoTIFFs and JSON telemetry to a Next.js frontend, where we render the scientific data interactively in the browser.

Project Source Code:

https://github.com/nillohitroy/space-visualizer

What benefits does it have?

Traditionally, analyzing SAR telemetry requires expensive desktop GIS software, high-end computers, and specialized training. The primary benefit of our platform is the total democratization of this data. By shifting the heavy mathematical processing to the cloud (CPU) and delivering the results to a browser, we allow decision-makers to access spatial intelligence instantly, with zero infrastructure overhead.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to turn raw physics into a ground-level survival tool. The impact is highly localized and deeply human:

Assam: We built an interactive TIF rendering engine that lets users slide between raw radar backscatter and AI-classified surface masks, visually proving how microwave signals pierce monsoon clouds to map hidden floodwaters.

Amazon: We integrated a dynamic time-series telemetry module that plots Radar Vegetation Index (RVI) against Earth Roughness, allowing users to track the exact mathematical drop in structural biomass that exposes under-canopy logging.

California: We engineered an interactive Cloude-Pottier H/α scatter chart that reads real radar pixels and plots them onto an Entropy-Alpha grid, letting users physically isolate surface scattering from volumetric changes caused by environmental stress.

How is our project creative?

Our creativity lies in how we bypassed traditional GIS bottlenecks and simplified complex physics. Instead of paying for expensive map servers, we engineered a GeoTIFF rendering engine using geotiff.js to paint raw radar tensors directly onto an HTML canvas. Furthermore, we translated abstract physics into an intuitive format: we built an interactive Cloude-Pottier H/α scatter chart that dynamically sampled real radar pixels and visually grouped them into physical scattering mechanisms, making eigenvalue decompositions instantly understandable for non-scientists.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

  • Data Pipeline & ML: Python, Kaggle, NASA earthaccess, ISRO Bhoonidhi API, xarray, dask (lazy memory management), h5py, and scikit-learn (K-Means clustering).
  • Frontend Framework: Next.js, Tailwind CSS.
  • Web Visualization: deck.gl (interactive 3D scrollytelling globe), recharts (telemetry graphs), geotiff.js (in-browser raster processing), and react-katex (mathematical typesetting).

What factors did our team consider?

We deeply considered the mindset of our end-user: disaster managers and local authorities who do not have the time to learn microwave physics during an active crisis. We prioritized actionability. Every data map in our UI is paired with clear, human-readable explanations of what is physically happening, what the radar signature means, and direct, actionable directives. We also factored in strict performance constraints—choosing to intelligently crop dense center patches from the radar swaths to ensure the web app remains lightning-fast.

Future Scope & Scalability

While our current pipeline successfully demonstrates the power of SAR data using on-demand cloud processing, our next development phase focuses on automation, scale, and predictive intelligence.

  • GPU-Accelerated Deep Learning & Generative AI: We plan to transition from our current clustering algorithms to dedicated GPU environments to train advanced machine learning models (such as CNNs for semantic segmentation). Additionally, we aim to integrate Generative AI to automatically analyze the processed radar tensors and draft plain-language disaster reports or alert summaries for local authorities.
  • Dynamic Backend & Predictive Forecasting: We will replace the static telemetry exports with a persistent, dynamic backend capable of continuously ingesting live satellite passes. By feeding this continuous data stream into predictive models, the system will move beyond just observing current conditions to actually forecasting future events—such as predicting the spread of floodwaters over the next 48 hours or estimating future subsidence rates.
  • On-Demand Regional Live-Mapping: Currently, our platform highlights predefined global hotspots. Our ultimate goal is to build a fully functional agentic system. A user will be able to draw a custom shape anywhere on the interactive globe, instantly triggering the backend to fetch, process, and render live SAR data for that specific region and the agent can conduct actions on the fly.
